questions.q: Couldn't the parser just raise an error when it finds nothing?
questions.a: No. Most replies legitimately have no tool call, so “nothing found” must be allowed. The check has to live where the right answer is known: a test with a prompt that must call a tool.

questions.q: When would you say the new model really is worse at tools?
questions.a: Only after the template and parser are proven to match. Then run both models on a fixed set of prompts with known correct calls and compare.
Problems that show up only in long conversations or with several calls at once. Add a case each time you find a gap.

questions.q: Which part of tool calling stayed the same in the swap, and which part changed?
questions.a: The tool definitions (standard JSON) stayed the same. The markup the model writes when it calls a tool changed, because each family learned its own style.

questions.q: Why does the agent loop stop instead of crashing?
questions.a: It sees no tool calls and a normal finish reason, which is exactly what a finished answer looks like, so it returns the text as the final reply.

teach.title: How it works: finding it and fencing it off

questions.q: Name the three things you'd version together, and the test that guards them.
questions.a: The model version, its chat template and its tool-call parser. The guard is a canary test that fails the deploy if a known prompt stops producing a parsed tool call.
